title: The midwives (Exodus 1:15–21)
hook: Shiphrah and Puah refuse to kill the boys; they feared God more than Pharaoh

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemot: a new king who knew not Joseph, and lives made bitter with brick and mortar. Your line was someone forgot. What did you find out about who made your things? Day three hundred seventy-eight.

Forced labor hasn't worked. The Israelites keep growing. So the king tries something worse, and quieter. He calls in two midwives, the women who sit with mothers in labor and catch the babies. He gives them an order: when you deliver a Hebrew woman, look. If it's a son, kill him. If it's a daughter, let her live. A death at a birth could pass for natural. It's an order given in private by the king of Egypt to two women with no power at all. And the Bible, which never tells us this Pharaoh's name, tells us theirs.
screen: `FORCED LABOR FAILS.` → `A PRIVATE ORDER.` → `IF IT'S A SON, KILL HIM.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "the name of the one was Shiphrah, and the name of the other Puah." Then the sentence that makes them unforgettable: "But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive." They feared God. Here, that fear isn't panic. It's knowing whose word counts for more than the king's. The king calls them back: why have you let the boys live? And they have an answer ready. The Hebrew women aren't like Egyptian women, they say. They're lively. The babies are born before we even get there. Was it true? Was it a clever excuse? The text doesn't say, and readers, Christian and Jewish, still debate it. What the text does say is that God dealt well with them, and gave them households of their own. The Hebrew can be read as Hebrew midwives, or as midwives to the Hebrews, so we don't even know for certain which people they came from. Some ancient Jewish teachers thought they were Moses's own mother and sister. What we do know is that the story of the way out begins with two women saying no. Not with an army. Not with a prophet. With two professionals quietly refusing to do harm. This week has been full of people choosing: Judah choosing to stay instead of the boy, Joseph choosing not to take revenge, Jacob choosing to go. And now, at the start of a new book, Shiphrah and Puah choosing life.
screen: `SHIPHRAH AND PUAH, BY NAME.` · `THE MIDWIVES FEARED GOD.` · `THE HEBREW WOMEN ARE LIVELY.` · `GOD DEALT WELL WITH THEM.` · then, large: `AND SAVED THE MEN CHILDREN ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone who quietly said no to wrong. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who refused to go along with something they knew was wrong: a nurse, a teacher, a coworker, a grandparent, a stranger in a story you heard once. Maybe nobody thanked them. Maybe nobody even knew. Say their name to yourself, the way the Bible says Shiphrah and Puah. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If you don't, simply honor them in your heart. The bell holds the time.
The midwives. Shiphrah and Puah, who were ordered by Pharaoh to kill the Hebrew baby boys, feared God, and let them live.
Your line: two women said no. Today, tell someone about a person who quietly did the right thing, and say their name out loud. Day three hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Christians and Jews tell the story of Shiphrah and Puah as an example of refusing an unjust order, and the two are named in sermons on conscience and courage.

fork.setup: you're a midwife. the king of Egypt himself orders you, in private, to kill every Hebrew boy you deliver. what do you do?

run away from Egypt that night.

original.note: Hebrew: Shiphrah, one of the two midwives the text names, while the king stays nameless.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses is the first hero of Exodus.
what it means: the first heroes are two midwives who refused a king's order and let the babies live.
what a scholar hears: the Hebrew can mean Hebrew midwives or midwives to the Hebrews, so their own people is uncertain; the Talmud records a view that they were Jochebed and Miriam.
recall: where Jacob first saw God's face

notes: Week-end look-back (days 372–377) folded into the end of the teach.
Sotah 11b identifies Shiphrah and Puah with Jochebed and Miriam (one view; another says Jochebed and Elisheba). Confirm.
Whether the midwives' answer was truthful (1:19) has been debated (e.g. Augustine on lying). Stated as debated without ranking.
Shiphrah possibly from a root meaning 'beautiful/fair': common but not certain; confirm or set original to null.
'Gave them households' paraphrases KJV 'he made them houses' (1:21).
